"Go down" is a phrasal verb — a combination of a verb ("go") and a small word ("down") that together create a meaning different from, or richer than, the words alone. This is very common in English. The word down here almost always signals movement to a lower position, a lower level, or a lower state — whether that is physical, numerical, social, or metaphorical.

Because English uses phrasal verbs constantly, "go down" appears in dozens of situations.
Meaning 1: Physical Movement to a Lower Place

The most basic meaning. Something or someone moves from a higher position to a lower one.

  • She went down the stairs carefully.
  • The lift went down to the basement.
  • He bent down and went down on his knees to pick it up.

This is the core, literal meaning. Everything else grows from this root idea of "descending" or "moving lower."
Meaning 2: The Sun Setting

When the sun "goes down," it sets — it moves below the horizon at the end of the day. This is one of the oldest uses of the phrase.

  • We watched the sun go down over the ocean.
  • Let's finish the work before the sun goes down.
  • The sky turns orange when the sun goes down.

You will often also hear "sundown" as a single noun meaning sunset — this came directly from "the sun goes down."
Meaning 3: A Decrease in Numbers, Levels, or Quality

When a price, number, temperature, or standard becomes lower or worse, it "goes down." This is extremely common in everyday speech.

  • The price of onions went down after the harvest.
  • The temperature went down sharply at night.
  • Petrol prices have gone down this week.
  • The quality of their food has really gone down lately. (meaning it has become worse)
  • Crime in the city went down by 20% last year.

Notice that in this meaning, the opposite is "go up." If something improves or increases, it "goes up." If it worsens or decreases, it "goes down."
Meaning 4: A Computer, Website, or System Stops Working

When a machine, server, website, or any technical system stops functioning, we say it "goes down." This meaning is very common in the modern world of technology.

  • The website went down for three hours because of a technical problem.
  • Our internet went down during the storm.
  • The company's servers went down last night.
  • The app is down right now — it must have gone down an hour ago.

Notice that after the system stops working, people often say "it is down" (not "it is going down"). "Goes down" refers to the moment it stops; "is down" refers to the period while it remains broken.
Meaning 5: How Something Is Received by People

This meaning is about how an audience, group, or person reacts to something — a speech, a joke, a new rule, a decision, a performance. If people like it or accept it positively, it "goes down well." If they dislike it or react badly, it "goes down badly" or "doesn't go down well."

  • His speech went down very well with the crowd. (the crowd loved it)
  • The new policy didn't go down well with the workers. (the workers hated it)
  • Her joke went down badly — nobody laughed.
  • How did the news go down with your family? (How did your family react to the news?)

This meaning is very commonly used in British English, though it is understood everywhere. Think of it as: how did something "land" with the audience?
Meaning 6: To Be Remembered or Recorded in History

When someone or something "goes down in history," they become permanently remembered — usually for doing something remarkable, important, or notorious.

  • This day will go down in history as one of the greatest ever.
  • She will go down in history as the first woman to climb that mountain.
  • He went down in history as the man who changed everything.
  • That match will go down as one of the greatest finals ever played.

You can also say "go down as" without "history" to mean "be remembered or described as":

  • He went down as one of the worst leaders the company ever had.
Meaning 7: A Ship, Plane, or Vehicle Sinking or Crashing

When a ship sinks or a plane crashes into the sea or ground, it "goes down."

  • The ship went down after hitting the rocks.
  • The Titanic went down in the North Atlantic in 1912.
  • The small aircraft went down in the mountains.

This is a natural extension of the physical meaning — the vessel literally moves downward into the water or ground.
Meaning 8: To Be Defeated or to Lose

In sports and competitions, if a team or player is beaten, they "go down." This is used in journalism and sports commentary frequently.

  • The team went down 2–0 against their rivals.
  • The champion went down in the third round. (was knocked out or defeated)
  • They went down fighting but eventually lost.

It can also describe being knocked to the ground:

  • The boxer went down after a heavy punch.

Additionally, in British football (soccer), when a team is relegated — meaning they drop to a lower division at the end of a season — they are said to "go down."

  • Three teams will go down at the end of this season.
Meaning 9: Something Happening (American Informal)

In informal American English, "go down" can mean "to happen" or "to take place," often referring to something suspicious, dramatic, or noteworthy.

  • What's going down? (What is happening? What's going on?)
  • Something strange is going down in that building.
  • Do you know what went down last night? (Do you know what happened last night?)

You might hear this in films, music, or casual American conversation. It has a slightly street or urban feel to it.
Meaning 10: To Go to Prison (British Informal)

In British informal English, if someone "goes down," it can mean they are sent to prison.

  • He went down for ten years for robbery. (He was sentenced to ten years in prison.)
  • If they find him guilty, he'll go down.

This is informal and mainly British. You would hear it in British films and TV shows. The phrase suggests the person is "going down" into a lower, darker place — the prison.
Meaning 11: To Travel Somewhere "Lower" or Farther Away

In British English especially, "go down" is used to describe traveling south, to the city centre, or to a place considered less important or simply farther away. The opposite — traveling north or to a more important place — would be "go up."

  • We're going down to London this weekend. (traveling from the north of England to London)
  • I'll go down to the shops and get some milk.
  • He went down to the village to buy bread.

This use of "down" to mean "toward the centre" or "to a smaller place" is part of a broader cultural and geographical way of speaking in British English.
Meaning 12: Food or Drink Being Swallowed

When food or drink "goes down," it passes through your throat when you eat or drink it. This often appears in comments about how easy or pleasant it was to swallow.

  • That tea went down nicely. (It was pleasant to drink.)
  • The pill didn't go down easily — it got stuck in my throat.
  • A hot bowl of soup really goes down well on a cold day.
  • The medicine went down smoothly with a glass of water.
Meaning 13: To Become Ill with Something — "Go Down With"

When you add "with" after "go down," it means to become sick with an illness.

  • Half the office went down with flu last week.
  • She went down with food poisoning after the party.
  • He went down with a fever on the day of his exam.

This is primarily British English. In American English, people are more likely to say "came down with."
A Very Important Warning — "Go Down On"

You must know this. In informal English, "go down on someone" is a sexual expression — it means to perform oral sex on a person. This meaning is well-known among native speakers.

Why does this matter to you as a learner? Because if you ever accidentally say something like "I went down on my boss to thank him" when you meant "I knelt down in front of my boss to pick something up," the results could be extremely embarrassing.

Always be careful with how you use "go down on" in a sentence. The safest rule: avoid "go down on" in professional or formal settings unless you are certain of the context.
A Summary of All the Meanings

Here is a clear recap, written in plain words:

Go down means...

  1. To move physically to a lower place — go down the stairs
  2. The sun setting at the end of the day — the sun goes down
  3. A number, price, or quality becoming lower or worse — prices went down
  4. A system or machine stopping to work — the server went down
  5. How something is received by an audience — the speech went down well
  6. To be remembered in history — go down in history
  7. A ship or plane sinking or crashing — the ship went down
  8. To be defeated — the team went down 3–0
  9. To happen (American informal) — what's going down?
  10. To go to prison (British informal) — he went down for five years
  11. To travel somewhere south or farther away (British) — going down to London
  12. Food or drink being swallowed — the soup went down nicely
  13. "Go down with" — to become ill — she went down with fever
  14. "Go down on" — a sexual expression (use carefully)
How to Remember All This

The key insight is that almost every meaning of "go down" carries the same underlying idea: something is moving to a lower state, lower place, lower number, or lower condition. The sun descends. Prices descend. A reputation descends. A system falls. A person falls in a fight. Even being "received well" uses the metaphor of something landing softly.

Once you feel this root idea of descent or reduction, the many meanings become far easier to understand, remember, and use correctly.
